title: Слово о пълку Игоревѣ
titleEn: The Tale of Igor's Campaign — IX: Igor's escape
draftNote: Part IX — Igor's escape (a fresh source paragraph): God shows Igor the way home; the famous «Igor sleeps, Igor watches» triad; the crux «Комонь въ полуночи»; the flight itself as a chain of animal transformations (ermine, wolf, falcon) shared with the Polovtsian Ovlur; the river Donets addresses Igor and he answers in kind, invoking by contrast the river Stugna and the 1093 drowning of Prince Rostislav Vsevolodovich; the birds fall silent to shield the fugitives while woodpecker and nightingale guide them; and the part closes with Gzak and Konchak's riddling exchange over what to do about Igor's son, left behind as a hostage.
source: Text: editio princeps — «Ироическая пѣснь о походѣ на половцовъ удѣльнаго князя Новагорода-Сѣверскаго Игоря Святославича», ed. A. I. Musin-Pushkin, Moscow, 1800 (public domain); via Russian Wikisource. 1800 orthography preserved. Prose sense-units at the edition's punctuation (no imposed verse lineation). Transliteration: scholarly Slavist romanization (ž š č c x; ě = ѣ; ŭ / ĭ = ъ / ь). Pronunciation: reconstructed late-12th-c. Old East Slavic (see slovo-audio doc); ж/ш/ц read hard by convention. Translations made fresh from the 1800 original.
about: Igor's escape from Polovtsian captivity, aided by a Christian Polovtsian named Ovlur (spelled Овлуръ/Влуръ within this same passage). Fleeing by night as a chain of animal transformations — ermine, wolf, then falcon — Igor crosses to the river Donets, which speaks to him and is answered in kind; his praise of the Donets turns to an implicit rebuke of the river Stugna, recalling the historical 1093 drowning of the young Prince Rostislav Vsevolodovich, a defeat also recorded in the Primary Chronicle. The pursuing khans Gzak and Konchak, unable to catch Igor himself, debate in a riddling exchange what to do with his son Vladimir, left a hostage in the Polovtsian camp. As throughout the poem, several lines here are genuine dark places — the truncated «Комонь въ полуночи», the elliptical «Князю Игорю не быть», the debated «стругы ростре на кусту» — and are flagged as unresolved rather than translated with invented confidence. The poem survives in no manuscript (the single copy burned in 1812), so no reading here claims more certainty than the 1800 print itself supports.

sentences.t: Прысну море полунощи; идутъ сморци мьглами;
sentences.tr: Prysnu more polunošči; idutŭ smorci mĭglami;
sentences.l: The sea gasped at midnight; mist-whirls move through the fogs;
sentences.i: At midnight the sea gave a gasp; whirls of mist go stirring through the fog;
sentences.n: This opens a new source paragraph and the poem's escape movement. Прысну is an aorist (a single sudden 'burst, gasp, splash'). сморци is a rare word, attested almost nowhere else in Old East Slavic — 'waterspouts' or 'whirls/columns of mist' is the conventional rendering, kept here, but the word itself is genuinely uncertain, of the same order as part I's «стазби». The natural world, ominous through most of the poem, now moves in Igor's favor — the sea and mist mask his flight rather than foretell his doom.

sentences.t: Игореви Князю Богъ путь кажетъ изъ земли Половецкой на землю Рускую, къ отню злату столу.
sentences.tr: Igorevi Knjazju Bogŭ putĭ kažetŭ izŭ zemli Poloveckoj na zemlju Ruskuju, kŭ otnju zlatu stolu.
sentences.l: To Igor the Prince, God shows the way, out of the Polovtsian land onto the Russian land, to [his] father's golden seat.
sentences.i: God shows Prince Igor the way out of the Polovtsian land and back into the land of Rus', to his father's golden throne.
sentences.n: The first direct statement in the poem that God himself favors Igor's escape — a rare moment where the Christian God, rather than the pagan omens and beast-spirits that dominate the campaign narrative, intervenes. «отню злату столу», 'father's golden seat' — стол in Old Rus' political language means a prince's seat of rule; Igor's own patrimony was Novgorod-Seversk, inherited from his father Svyatoslav Olgovich. «изъ ... на ...» marks the direction of the journey exactly: out of Cuman land, onto Rus' land.

sentences.t: Погасоша вечеру зари: Игорь спитъ, Игорь бдитъ, Игорь мыслію поля мѣритъ отъ великаго Дону до малаго Донца.
sentences.tr: Pogasoša večeru zari: Igorĭ spitŭ, Igorĭ bditŭ, Igorĭ mysliju polja měritŭ otŭ velikago Donu do malago Donca.
sentences.l: In the evening the glows went out: Igor sleeps, Igor keeps watch, Igor measures the steppe in thought from the great Don to the small Donets.
sentences.i: By evening the afterglow had faded: Igor sleeps, yet Igor is watchful — in his mind he measures the steppe from the great Don to the little Donets.
sentences.n: Погасоша is an aorist 3rd plural, its subject the plural «зари» ('the [sunset] glows'); «вечеру» is dative used adverbially, 'in the evening.' The triad «Игорь спитъ, Игорь бдитъ, Игорь мыслію...» is a tight, paradoxical anaphora — asleep yet alert — built on bare present-tense verbs. мыслію ('in/by thought,' instrumental) echoes the proem's own most debated line, Boyan's «растѣкашется мыслію по древу» — here it is Igor's own mind, not a bard's, that ranges over the land. великаго Дону recalls the campaign's original goal in part I («да позримъ синего Дону»); малаго Донца is the Seversky Donets, the smaller river along which Igor actually now flees, and which the poem personifies two units later.

sentences.t: Комонь въ полуночи.
sentences.tr: Komonĭ vŭ polunoči.
sentences.l: A steed, at midnight.
sentences.i: A horse — at midnight.
sentences.n: The poem's single most notoriously truncated line, a genuine dark place flagged here rather than resolved: a bare nominal phrase, with no verb at all, echoing unit 1's own 'at midnight.' No reading commands consensus — proposals range from treating it as an elliptical stage-direction ('[he mounts] a horse at midnight'), to a fragment of a longer clause lost to a printer's or copyist's slip, to genuine, unrecoverable corruption (the manuscript itself is gone, so nothing can be checked against it). We print it exactly as it stands in the 1800 edition and supply no implied verb.

sentences.t: Овлуръ свисну за рѣкою; велить Князю разумѣти.
sentences.tr: Ovlurŭ svisnu za rěkoju; velitĭ Knjazju razuměti.
sentences.l: Ovlur whistled beyond the river; he bids the prince understand.
sentences.i: Beyond the river Ovlur gave a whistle, signaling the prince to grasp his meaning.
sentences.n: Ovlur (spelled Овлуръ here, Влуръ two sentences on — one figure, the printed spelling shifting within this same passage) is the Polovtsian who helps Igor escape; the poem says nothing more of him here, but he is usually identified by scholars with a similarly-described helper in the parallel chronicle account of these same events, likewise said to have had a Christian, Rus' mother — though names and spellings differ between the two sources. свисну is an aorist (one whistled signal); велить is present tense, a small tense-shift within the same sentence easy to pass over.

sentences.t: Князю Игорю не быть: кликну стукну земля; въшумѣ трава.
sentences.tr: Knjazju Igorju ne bytĭ: kliknu stuknu zemlja; vŭšumě trava.
sentences.l: For Prince Igor [it was] not to be [held]: the earth gave a shout, a knock; the grass rustled.
sentences.i: Prince Igor was not to be held: a cry, a knock — the earth resounded; the grass stirred.
sentences.n: A second compressed, elliptical line, of a kind with unit 4's crux. «не быть» is an infinitive in an impersonal dative construction — Князю Игорю (dative) + не быть, 'it is not to be, for Prince Igor, [that he remain a captive]' — the very same pattern as the poem's own opening line, «Не лѣполи ны бяшетъ ... начяти» (dative + a form of быти). кликну, стукну are aorists, a rhymed onomatopoeic pair ('there sounded a cry, a knock') for the sudden commotion of the escape; въшумѣ (aorist) 'rustled, made a noise' — whose noise (Igor's own flight, or an alarm behind him) the text does not say.

sentences.t: Вежи ся Половецкіи подвизашася;
sentences.tr: Veži sja Poloveckii podvizašasja;
sentences.l: The Polovtsian tent-camps were set into motion;
sentences.i: The Polovtsian camp broke into commotion;
sentences.n: вежа = a tent, yurt or camp-wagon of the nomadic Polovtsians, their mobile settlements. подвизашася is an aorist reflexive, 'stirred, were roused, were set moving' — read here, in context, as the alarm spreading once Igor's flight is discovered, though the bare verb is neutral enough that some take it simply as the camp breaking camp to move.

sentences.t: а Игорь Князь поскочи горнастаемъ къ тростію, и бѣлымъ гоголемъ на воду;
sentences.tr: a Igorĭ Knjazĭ poskoči gornastaemŭ kŭ trostiju, i bělymŭ gogolemŭ na vodu;
sentences.l: and Prince Igor darted as an ermine to the reeds, and as a white golden-eye onto the water;
sentences.i: and Prince Igor darted off — an ermine to the reeds, a white goldeneye onto the water;
sentences.n: The escape becomes a chain of animal transformations, each cast in the instrumental 'comparison' case (горнастаемъ, гоголемъ, 'as an ermine,' 'as a golden-eye'), the same construction Boyan's own shape-changing used in the proem («сѣрымъ вълкомъ», 'as a grey wolf'; «шизымъ орломъ», 'as a dusky eagle'). горнастай = ermine/stoat; гоголь = the common goldeneye, a diving duck whose flash of white plumage suits a swimmer vanishing into the water. поскочи is an aorist.

sentences.t: въвръжеся на бръзъ комонь, и скочи съ него босымъ влъкомъ, и потече къ лугу Донца, и полетѣ соколомъ подъ мьглами избивая гуси и лебеди, завтроку, и обѣду и ужинѣ.
sentences.tr: vŭvrŭžesja na brŭzŭ komonĭ, i skoči sŭ nego bosymŭ vlŭkomŭ, i poteče kŭ lugu Donca, i poletě sokolomŭ podŭ mĭglami izbivaja gusi i lebedi, zavtroku, i obědu i užině.
sentences.l: he threw himself upon a swift steed, and leapt from it as a barefoot wolf, and ran on to the meadow of the Donets, and flew as a falcon beneath the mists, striking down geese and swans, for breakfast, and for dinner and for supper.
sentences.i: he flung himself onto a swift horse, sprang down off it as a wolf on his own bare feet, ran on to the Donets meadow, and flew as a falcon under the mist, striking down geese and swans — breakfast, dinner, and supper all in one flight.
sentences.n: The transformation-chain climbs: horse, then wolf (босымъ, literally 'barefoot, unshod' — the wolf runs on its own legs, no longer mounted, a small pointed pun right after the horse is abandoned), then falcon, hunting birds the whole way. «завтроку, и обѣду и ужинѣ» (dative, 'for breakfast, and for dinner and supper') compresses a full day's headlong flight into one breath, and lets Igor himself now play the falcon that Boyan, in the proem, could only imagine loosing on a flock of swans.

sentences.t: Коли Игорь соколомъ полетѣ, тогда Влуръ влъкомъ потече, труся собою студеную росу; претръгоста бо своя бръзая комоня.
sentences.tr: Koli Igorĭ sokolomŭ poletě, togda Vlurŭ vlŭkomŭ poteče, trusja soboju studenuju rosu; pretrŭgosta bo svoja brŭzaja komonja.
sentences.l: When Igor flew as a falcon, then Vlur ran as a wolf, shaking off from himself the cold dew; for the two of them had strained their own swift steeds.
sentences.i: As Igor flew like a falcon, Vlur ran alongside like a wolf, shaking the cold dew from his own coat — for between them they had ridden their swift horses to exhaustion.
sentences.n: Ovlur now shares Igor's shape-shifting (spelled Влуръ here, against Овлуръ earlier — the same figure, kept as printed each time). претръгоста is a DUAL aorist — the -ста ending marks exactly two subjects, the same dual number as «есвѣ», used of Igor and Vsevolod together in part I — a form modern Russian has lost entirely. It binds Igor and Ovlur together as a pair and explains, in one word, why both men have left their horses behind and gone on as wolf and falcon: their mounts had given out under them.

sentences.t: Донецъ рече: Княже Игорю! не мало ти величія, а Кончаку нелюбія, а Руской земли веселіа.
sentences.tr: Donecŭ reče: Knjaže Igorju! ne malo ti veličija, a Končaku neljubija, a Ruskoj zemli veselia.
sentences.l: The Donets said: Prince Igor! not little is there of glory to you, and of displeasure to Konchak, and of gladness to the Russian land.
sentences.i: The Donets spoke: 'Prince Igor! Great is your glory, great Konchak's displeasure, and great the joy of the Russian land!'
sentences.n: The river Donets is personified and speaks directly to Igor — a river-dialogue that answers, in reverse, Yaroslavna's own address to the Dnepr in part VIII (there she speaks first; here the river speaks first). «не мало» + genitive is a litotes ('not a little of...' = 'a great deal of'), struck three times in one breath — Igor's glory, Konchak's displeasure, Rus's rejoicing. нелюбіе, literally 'non-love,' means displeasure, ill-will. Кончакъ (Konchak) is the historically attested Polovtsian khan who had held Igor captive, and returns at this part's close.

sentences.t: Игорь рече, о Донче! не мало ти величія, лелѣявшу Князя на влънахъ, стлавшу ему зелѣну траву на своихъ сребреныхъ брезѣхъ, одѣвавшу его теплыми мъглами подъ сѣнію зелену древу;
sentences.tr: Igorĭ reče, o Donče! ne malo ti veličija, lelějavšu Knjazja na vlŭnaxŭ, stlavšu jemu zelěnu travu na svoixŭ srebrenyxŭ brezěxŭ, oděvavšu jego teplymi mŭglami podŭ sěniju zelenu drevu;
sentences.l: Igor said, O Donets! not little is there of glory to you, who cradled the prince on the waves, who spread for him green grass on your own silvery banks, who clothed him with warm mists under the shade of a green tree;
sentences.i: Igor answered: 'O Donets! Great is your glory too — you cradled the prince on your waves, spread green grass for him on your silver banks, wrapped him in warm mists beneath the shade of a green tree;
sentences.n: Igor answers in kind, throwing the river's own litotes back at it. лелѣявшу, стлавшу, одѣвавшу are dative singular participles agreeing with «ти» ('to you') — a chain of dative appositions describing the river's own past kindnesses, a construction with no easy modern equivalent ('to you, the one who cradled...'). лелѣяти ('to cradle, nurse') is the same verb used of the Kurian warriors 'cradled under helmets' in part I, and of Yaroslavna's own plea to this same river in part VIII («лелѣялъ еси... носады») — the image threads all three passages together.

sentences.t: стрежаше е гоголемъ на водѣ, чайцами на струяхъ, Чрьнядьми на ветрѣхъ.
sentences.tr: strežaše e gogolemŭ na vodě, čajcami na strujaxŭ, Črĭnjadĭmi na vetrěxŭ.
sentences.l: [it] guarded him with the golden-eye on the water, with gulls on the currents, with black ducks on the winds.
sentences.i: and you watched over him — with the goldeneye on the water, with gulls on the currents, with black ducks riding the winds.
sentences.n: стрежаше is an imperfect ('kept watch, guarded' — a sustained or repeated past action, set against the aorists around it). е is the old enclitic accusative of the third-person pronoun, 'him' (the ancestor of modern его in this role). Three waterfowl again stand sentinel, echoing unit 8's own goldeneye-transformation: гоголь (goldeneye duck), чайка (gull), чрьнядь (a dark diving duck, likely the scaup or pochard) — a small natural-history catalogue of the river's watchful birds.

sentences.t: Не тако ли, рече, рѣка Стугна худу струю имѣя, пожръши чужи ручьи, и стругы ростре на кусту?
sentences.tr: Ne tako li, reče, rěka Stugna xudu struju iměja, požrŭši čuži ručĭi, i strugy rostre na kustu?
sentences.l: Was it not otherwise, [Igor] said, [with] the river Stugna, having a poor stream, having swallowed up others' streams, and scattered its rills upon the thicket?
sentences.i: 'Was it not otherwise,' he said, 'with the river Stugna — a thin stream in itself, yet one that swallowed up other, stranger currents, and spread its waters wide over the brush?'
sentences.n: Igor turns from praising the Donets to an implicit reproach of a different river, the Stugna, by contrast ('Не тако ли,' 'was it not otherwise,' i.e. 'unlike you'). This opens a flashback exemplum to 1093: Prince Rostislav Vsevolodovich of Pereyaslavl drowned fleeing a defeat by the Polovtsians on the Stugna, a real event recorded in the Primary Chronicle; his brother, the future Vladimir Monomakh, tried in vain to save him. «стругы ростре на кусту» ('scattered its rills/currents on the bush') is itself a genuine dark place — usually read as the swollen Stugna spreading destructively over the bank-side scrub in flood, setting up the drowning that follows, but the precise sense of «стругы» and «на кусту» here is debated, not settled.

sentences.t: Уношу Князю Ростиславу затвори Днѣпрь темнѣ березѣ.
sentences.tr: Unošu Knjazju Rostislavu zatvori Dněprĭ temně berezě.
sentences.l: For the young Prince Rostislav, the Dnepr shut [him] on the dark bank.
sentences.i: For young Prince Rostislav, the Dnepr closed over him on the dark bank.
sentences.n: The flashback continues, but names the Dnepr, not the Stugna, as the river that closed over Rostislav; the Stugna is in fact a right-bank tributary of the Dnepr, so this may be the poet using 'Dnepr' loosely for the whole river system, or simply conflating the two rivers — either way, the underlying event (Rostislav's drowning in 1093) is historically real even where the poem's own river-name is imprecise. уноша = 'young man, youth' (dative уношу).

sentences.t: Плачется мати Ростиславя по уноши Князи Ростиславѣ.
sentences.tr: Plačetsja mati Rostislavja po unoši Knjazi Rostislavě.
sentences.l: Rostislav's mother weeps for the young Prince Rostislav.
sentences.i: Rostislav's mother weeps for her young son, Prince Rostislav.
sentences.n: A second grieving mother in the poem, its pathos turning from the drowned prince to the one left mourning him — the same move the poem makes with Svyatoslav's dream-grief in part V and, most famously, with Yaroslavna's lament in part VIII. Rostislav Vsevolodovich was historically a younger brother of Vladimir Monomakh; nothing more is known of their mother from the chronicles, and the poem supplies no name.

sentences.t: Уныша цвѣты жалобою, и древо стугою къ земли прѣклонило, а не сорокы втроскоташа.
sentences.tr: Unyša cvěty žaloboju, i drevo stugoju kŭ zemli prěklonilo, a ne soroky vtroskotaša.
sentences.l: The flowers drooped with lament, and the tree, with grief, bent [itself] to the ground — and [it was] not [that] magpies chattered.
sentences.i: The flowers wilted for grief, and the tree bowed down to the earth in sorrow — and no, it was not magpies chattering.
sentences.n: A famous, debated wordplay closes the exemplum: «стугою» ('with grief, with anguish,' from the OES noun туга/стуга) sounds like the river's own name, Стугна, just named two units before — whether the poet intends this as a deliberate pun (the river's name itself carrying an echo of sorrow) is argued rather than settled, and we keep the plain sense without asserting the pun as fact. The closing clause turns nature's mourning against folk superstition: magpie-chatter was popularly read as an omen, and the poet insists this grief is real grief, not a bird-sign — a suspicion of birds-as-false-witnesses that returns, inverted, in the very next unit's total silence of the birds.

sentences.t: На слѣду Игоревѣ ѣздитъ Гзакъ съ Кончакомъ.
sentences.tr: Na slědu Igorevě ězditŭ Gzakŭ sŭ Končakomŭ.
sentences.l: Along Igor's track ride Gzak with Konchak.
sentences.i: Along Igor's trail ride Gzak and Konchak.
sentences.n: The narrative returns from the Rostislav exemplum to the pursuit itself. Gzak (Кза/Гзакъ) and Konchak are both historically attested Polovtsian khans of the real 1185 campaign; Konchak had been Igor's own captor, and the two now hunt the escaped prince together, setting up the riddle-dialogue that closes this part.

sentences.t: Тогда врани не граахуть, галици помлъкоша, сорокы не троскоташа, полозію ползоша только, дятлове тектомъ путь къ рѣцѣ кажутъ, соловіи веселыми пѣсьми свѣтъ повѣдаютъ.
sentences.tr: Togda vrani ne graaxutĭ, galici pomlŭkoša, soroky ne troskotaša, poloziju polzoša tolĭko, djatlove tektomŭ putĭ kŭ rěcě kažutŭ, solovii veselymi pěsĭmi světŭ povědajutŭ.
sentences.l: Then the ravens did not caw, the jackdaws fell silent, the magpies did not chatter, only the grass-snakes crept, the woodpeckers with their tapping show the way to the river, the nightingales with joyful songs announce the light.
sentences.i: Then the ravens did not caw, the jackdaws held their tongues, the magpies did not chatter — only the grass-snakes stirred; the woodpeckers, tapping, point the way to the river, and the nightingales, with joyful songs, herald the dawn.
sentences.n: A deliberate inversion of the ill-omened bird-catalogue that opened the campaign in part I ('не буря соколы занесе... галици стады бѣжать'): there, birds forecast disaster; here, on the escape, the loud, alarm-raising birds — ravens, jackdaws, magpies — fall silent so as not to betray Igor, while the harmless woodpecker and nightingale actively help him, tapping out the river's direction and singing in the dawn. полозіе, 'grass-snakes' (a large, harmless steppe snake, cf. Elaphe/Zamenis), is an unusual detail — even the snakes go about quietly, reinforcing the total hush around the fugitive.

sentences.t: Млъвитъ Гзакъ Кончакови: аже соколъ къ гнѣзду летитъ, соколича рострѣляевѣ своими злачеными стрѣлами.
sentences.tr: Mlŭvitŭ Gzakŭ Končakovi: aže sokolŭ kŭ gnězdu letitŭ, sokoliča rostrěljaevě svoimi zlačenymi strělami.
sentences.l: Gzak speaks to Konchak: since the falcon flies to [its] nest, let us [two] shoot the falcon-chick with our gilded arrows.
sentences.i: Gzak says to Konchak: 'Since the falcon is flying home to its nest, let the two of us shoot down the falcon-chick with our gilded arrows.'
sentences.n: млъвити, 'to speak, murmur' (cf. modern молвить) — opens the closing riddle-dialogue between the two khans, built on two rounds of an identical opening line, «аже соколъ къ гнѣзду летитъ», spoken first by Gzak, then echoed by Konchak, before Gzak's own final rebuttal. The riddle's literal stakes: the escaped 'falcon' is Igor himself, flying home to Rus'; the 'falcon-chick' (соколичь) left in the nest is his young son, Vladimir Igorevich, still a hostage in Polovtsian hands. Gzak's proposal is a literal one — kill the boy in reprisal. рострѣляевѣ is a 1st-person DUAL verb (the -евѣ ending, 'we two shall shoot,' the same dual seen in part I's «есвѣ»), grammatically binding Gzak and Konchak together as the pair making this decision — a form with no equivalent in modern Russian's singular/plural-only verb system.

sentences.t: Рече Кончакъ ко Гзѣ: аже соколъ къ гнѣзду летитъ, а вѣ соколца опутаевѣ красною дивицею.
sentences.tr: Reče Končakŭ ko Gzě: aže sokolŭ kŭ gnězdu letitŭ, a vě sokolca oputaevě krasnoju diviceju.
sentences.l: Konchak said to Gzak: since the falcon flies to [its] nest, and let us [two] entangle the falcon-chick with a fair maiden.
sentences.i: Konchak said to Gzak: 'Since the falcon is flying home to its nest — let the two of us bind the falcon-chick with a fair maiden instead.'
sentences.n: Konchak's answer opens the second round of the exchange, repeating Gzak's own opening line before proposing the opposite course: marriage rather than killing, entangling the boy in Polovtsian ties through a bride instead of an arrow. опутаевѣ is again 1st-person dual ('we two shall entangle, ensnare'), matching рострѣляевѣ in the unit before. Chronicle history bears this out obliquely — Igor's son Vladimir Igorevich did later marry a daughter of Konchak's — though the poem itself narrates no more than this riddle. дивицею ('maiden,' spelled with и here) prints differently from дѣвицею/дѣвице (with ѣ) in the unit that follows, for the same word — kept exactly as printed, one more small spelling inconsistency of the 1800 edition.

sentences.t: И рече Гзакъ къ Кончакови: аще его опутаевѣ красною дѣвицею, ни нама будетъ сокольца, ни нама красны дѣвице, то почнутъ наю птици бити въ полѣ Половецкомъ.
sentences.tr: I reče Gzakŭ kŭ Končakovi: ašče jego oputaevě krasnoju děviceju, ni nama budetŭ sokolĭca, ni nama krasny děvice, to počnutŭ naju ptici biti vŭ polě Poloveckomŭ.
sentences.l: And Gzak said to Konchak: if we [two] entangle him with a fair maiden, neither will there be to us [two] the falcon-chick, nor to us [two] the fair maiden — then birds will begin to strike us [two] in the Polovtsian field.
sentences.i: And Gzak said to Konchak: 'If we ensnare him with a fair maiden, we shall have neither the falcon-chick nor the fair maiden — and the birds will fall on the two of us in the Polovtsian field.'
sentences.n: The third and final turn of the exchange: Gzak's rebuttal of Konchak's proposal, and the part's closing lines. нама (dative dual, 'to the two of us') and наю (accusative dual, 'the two of us') keep the dual number running through the whole exchange, still binding Gzak and Konchak as a pair — three more dual forms alongside the рострѣляевѣ/опутаевѣ of the two units before. The closing image, «почнутъ наю птици бити», 'birds will begin to strike us,' is proverb-like, and its precise force is debated: it may picture birds of prey turning on the khans themselves, a reversal of the falcon-hunt they were just plotting, or simply figure exposure and ruin in the open steppe — no single reading is asserted here as certain. Note also «аще» here against «аже» in the two preceding units for the same conjunction ('if, since') — another spelling variant kept exactly as printed rather than normalized.

glossary.влуръ: Влуръ — Vlur (nom. sg.); spelling variant of Овлуръ, the same Polovtsian helper
glossary.влъкомъ: вълкъ — wolf (instr. sg., 'as a wolf'; spelled влъкъ here)
glossary.втроскоташа: въстроскотати — chattered (aorist 3pl; prefixed variant of троскотати)
glossary.въвръжеся: въврещися — threw himself, flung himself (aorist 3sg reflexive)

glossary.до: до — up to, as far as (prep. + gen.)

glossary.имѣя: имѣти — having (present participle, 'having a poor stream')

glossary.кончакомъ: Кончакъ — with Konchak (instr. sg.); Polovtsian khan, Igor's former captor
